blocks.body: Planners commonly advise a cooling-off period — a few months in an insured savings account or Treasury bills — before large decisions. Its purpose is behavioral: sudden money invites rushed purchases and pressure from others, so ask anyone advising you how they are paid, for example by commission. Deposit insurance covers {{fig:fdic_standard_max_deposit}} per depositor, per bank, for each ownership category, so spread a larger sum across banks or hold Treasury bills. Three things cannot wait for the cooling-off period. If anyone in the household gets SSI, Medicaid, SNAP or housing help, a lump sum can end eligibility (SSI's resource limit is {{fig:ssi_resource_limit_individual}} for an individual), so report it and ask before moving the money; an ABLE account or a special-needs trust can sometimes keep a person with a disability eligible. Taxable windfalls — lottery or gambling wins, back pay, most legal settlements other than for physical injury or sickness — are income for the year, so set the tax aside; if too little was withheld, an estimated tax payment can help avoid an underpayment penalty. And a decision to disclaim an inheritance must generally be made in writing within 9 months and before you accept the asset; using it or directing what happens to it can count as accepting.
blocks.plain: Financial planners often suggest waiting a few months — with the money in an insured savings account or Treasury bills — before making big decisions. The point is about behavior: sudden money invites rushed purchases and pressure from other people, so ask anyone who advises you how they get paid, for example by commission. Deposit insurance covers {{fig:fdic_standard_max_deposit}} for each depositor at each bank, for each type of account ownership, so split a larger amount across banks or buy Treasury bills. Three things can't wait for that pause. If anyone in your household gets SSI, Medicaid, SNAP or housing help, a lump sum can end that help (SSI's limit on what you can own is {{fig:ssi_resource_limit_individual}} for one person), so report it and ask before you move the money; an ABLE account or a special-needs trust can sometimes keep a person with a disability eligible. Windfalls that are taxable — lottery or gambling wins, back pay, most legal settlements that are not for a physical injury or sickness — count as income for the year, so set the tax money aside; if not enough tax was withheld, paying estimated tax can help you avoid a penalty. And if you inherited the money and might turn it down (a "disclaimer"), you generally must do that in writing within 9 months and before you accept it; using the money or telling others what to do with it can count as accepting.

blocks.body: Cash, a brokerage account, an inherited IRA and a house are taxed differently. Inherited assets generally get a basis stepped up to value at the date of death, so selling soon after inheriting often produces little gain. The step-up does not apply to pre-tax retirement accounts such as a traditional IRA or 401(k); withdrawals from them are generally taxed as income. Most non-spouse beneficiaries of an inherited IRA must empty it within 10 years, and if the original owner had started required distributions, annual distributions are required during those years too. A non-spouse beneficiary cannot roll an inherited IRA into their own; move it only by direct trustee-to-trustee transfer into an account titled as inherited, because a check made out to you counts as a withdrawal and cannot be put back.
blocks.plain: Cash, a brokerage account, an inherited IRA and a house are taxed in different ways. Inherited things usually get a new cost basis equal to their value on the day of death (a "step-up"), so selling soon after you inherit often creates little taxable gain. Pre-tax retirement accounts, such as a traditional IRA or 401(k), do not get this step-up; money you take out of them is usually taxed as income. Most people who inherit an IRA from someone other than a spouse must empty it within 10 years. If the original owner had already started required withdrawals, you must also take yearly withdrawals during those years. If you inherit an IRA from someone other than a spouse, you can't roll it into your own IRA. Move it only by a direct transfer from one company to the other, into an account labeled as inherited; a check made out to you counts as a withdrawal and can't be put back.

blocks.body: A windfall does not need a new plan; it accelerates the existing one. Pay off high-interest debt, finish the emergency fund, then fill tax-advantaged space before taxable investing. Before paying an old debt in collections, check whether it is past your state's time limit for lawsuits; a partial payment, or even admitting the debt, may restart that clock. Your own 401(k) contributions can come only out of pay, so one route is to raise your deferral and cover the smaller paychecks from the windfall. A taxable windfall or a taxable withdrawal from an inherited IRA raises that year's income, which can reduce Marketplace premium tax credits that year and, two years later, raise Medicare premiums and lower federal student aid, so plan the timing of large withdrawals. If you get advance premium tax credits, report the higher income to the Marketplace, or you may have to pay back the difference at tax time.
blocks.plain: A windfall doesn't need a new plan — it speeds up the one you have. Pay off high-interest debt, finish the emergency fund, then fill tax-advantaged accounts before investing in a regular taxable account. Before you pay an old debt that is in collections, check whether it is past your state's time limit for being sued; paying part of it, or even admitting you owe it, may restart that clock. Your own 401(k) contributions can only come out of your paycheck, so one option is to raise your 401(k) contribution and use the windfall to cover the smaller paychecks. A taxable windfall, or taxable money taken out of an inherited IRA, raises your income for that year. That can shrink Marketplace premium tax credits that year and, two years later, raise Medicare premiums and lower federal student aid, so plan the timing of large withdrawals. If you get premium tax credits in advance, tell the Marketplace about the higher income, or you may have to pay back the difference when you file your taxes.

blocks.body: This choice applies only to money you are investing for the long term, after the debt and emergency-fund steps. Vanguard's historical study found that investing a lump sum immediately beat spreading it out over time in about two-thirds of rolling periods, because markets rise more often than they fall. Spreading it out buys protection against regret if the market drops soon after. Both are defensible; pick the one you will stick with.
blocks.plain: This choice is only for money you are investing for the long run, after you've paid down debt and built your emergency fund. Vanguard looked at past market history and found that investing a lump sum right away beat spreading it out over time in about two-thirds of the periods it studied, because markets go up more often than they go down. Spreading it out protects you from regret if the market falls right after you invest. Both are reasonable; choose the one you'll stick with.

blocks.body: Gifts above the annual exclusion ({{fig:gift_annual_exclusion}} per recipient for 2026) require a gift-tax return but rarely any tax, because they count against the lifetime exemption ({{fig:estate_exemption_individual}} per person for 2026). A gift to someone on SSI generally counts as their income and can reduce or end their benefit, and gifts made within five years before applying for Medicaid long-term care, such as a nursing home, can delay the giver's own coverage.
blocks.plain: If you give someone more than the yearly exclusion ({{fig:gift_annual_exclusion}} per person you give to, for 2026), you have to file a gift-tax return, but you rarely owe tax, because it counts against your lifetime exemption ({{fig:estate_exemption_individual}} for each giver, for 2026). A gift to someone who gets SSI usually counts as their income and can cut or end their SSI check. Gifts you make within five years before you apply for Medicaid to pay for long-term care, such as a nursing home, can delay your own coverage.
props: Gifts above the annual exclusion (per recipient) require a gift-tax return

Gifts within five years before applying for Medicaid long-term care can delay the giver's coverage

review.why: IRC 6654 computes the penalty per installment, so a single later payment may not remove the whole penalty; the body overstated and did not match the plain variant.

review.change: Dropped the clause "IRA contributions cannot exceed your earned income for the year".
review.why: Wrong as worded for a non-working spouse (a spousal IRA can be funded from the other spouse's compensation) and "earned income" is not the statutory "compensation"; the clause also did not lead to the 401(k) conclusion. The 401(k) mechanism alone carries CFP-36.

review.change: "a common route" -> "one route" (body) / "one option" (plain); "401(k) contributions come out of pay" -> "Your own 401(k) contributions can come only out of pay".
review.why: "Common" is a frequency claim with no primary source; employer contributions are not from pay, so the rule is scoped to the employee's own deferrals, as the IRS page states it.

source.quote: A traditional 401(k) plan allows eligible employees (i.e., employees eligible to participate in the plan) to make pre-tax elective deferrals through payroll deductions.

review.change: "Taxable windfalls and inherited IRA withdrawals raise that year's income" -> "A taxable windfall or a taxable withdrawal from an inherited IRA raises that year's income".
review.why: Qualified withdrawals from an inherited Roth IRA, and the basis portion of a traditional IRA, are not income; the unscoped wording contradicted the character block. Pub. 559 makes the traditional IRA distribution taxable only up to the decedent's taxable balance.

source.quote: The distribution is taxable in the year received as income in respect of a decedent up to the decedent's taxable balance.

review.why: CFP-35's Marketplace point is only half there without it: for a low-income reader the costly trap is repaying advance credits at filing, and the cure (report the change) is an action, not a lecture.
